cases.rationale: getHeader is a source; taint flows tenant -> id (assignment) -> query (string concat) -> executeQuery, all intra-procedural, so the engine should flag it.
getParameter taint reaches target through a ternary whose then-branch is the tainted host, then concatenates into Runtime.exec, which the documented model should still catch.
trim() and toLowerCase() are pass-through string ops that preserve taint, so the LDAP filter passed to DirContext.search stays tainted and should be flagged.
String.format is a listed pass-through op so the tainted username propagates into expr and reaches XPath.evaluate(arg0), which the model treats as a sink.

BufferedReader.readLine is a source; the StringBuilder member chain has a tainted append(order) arg, so toString() yields tainted sql passed to prepareStatement(arg0) — caught per the documented append-member rule.
Taint is stored into a Map via put and re-read via get; the documented model does not track taint through collections/maps, so the ProcessBuilder sink is a genuine miss.
System.getProperty is a source; taint concatenates into hql and flows to Hibernate createQuery, a documented SQLI sink, all within one method.
getParameter taint survives replace() (a pass-through, not a sanitizer) and '+' concat into new File(), a documented path sink, so intra-procedural taint should fire.
getHeader taint propagates through trim() and substring() (both listed pass-throughs) into Paths.get and Files.readAllBytes, which are documented path sinks.
getParameter taint reaches new URL() and openConnection() through a simple '+' concatenation chain, both documented SSRF sinks under the intra-procedural model.
getHeader taint survives toLowerCase() and concat, flowing into RestTemplate.getForObject, a documented SSRF sink; classic Host-header SSRF that stays fully intra-procedural.
BufferedReader.readLine() is a documented source; its taint flows through trim() into new URL().openConnection(), so the request-body-driven SSRF should be caught intra-procedurally.

The tainted getParameter value is passed as an argument to a separate method where the new File sink lives, and the documented model is intra-procedural only, so this cross-method flow is a genuine miss.

The open-redirect 'next' parameter is stored in a field in one method and read into the new URL sink in another, hitting both the field-storage and cross-method limitations, so it is an honest false negative.

MD5 is genuinely weak, but the literal is lowercase 'md5'; if the rule matches the exact strings "MD5"/"SHA-1" case-sensitively it misses this common casing variant, so it is a genuine false negative beyond the documented model.
Canonical weak-hash usage with the exact documented literal "SHA-1" passed directly to MessageDigest.getInstance, which the rule targets by design (true positive).
Cipher.getInstance receives a string literal containing both DES and ECB, both explicitly listed as weak-cipher triggers, so a case-sensitive match on these tokens fires (true positive).

Still weak DES-in-ECB, but the transformation string uses mixed casing 'Des/ecb'; if the rule token-matches the uppercase forms DES/ECB case-sensitively it misses this valid JCE-accepted casing, a genuine miss.
Directly constructs new Random() and uses it to build a session identifier, matching the exact 'new java.util.Random()' trigger for security-sensitive randomness (true positive).

Cryptographically weak because SeededRandom extends java.util.Random, but the security-relevant constructor is 'new SeededRandom(...)', not 'new Random()'/'Math.random()'; resolving the subclass to its weak parent is beyond the constructor-name match, so it is missed.

Although the ObjectInputStream is created inside a helper method, the literal 'new ObjectInputStream(...)' node still appears in the source and the rule flags that constructor wherever it occurs, so an AST scan detects it (true positive).

True positive: DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() with only setNamespaceAware/setValidating/setIgnoringComments/setCoalescing and zero setFeature/setAttribute calls, so no real XXE hardening is present.
True positive: SAXParserFactory.newInstance() with only an unrelated setNamespaceAware(true) setter and no setFeature/setAttribute hardening against external entities or DTDs.
True positive: anonymous X509TrustManager whose checkClientTrusted and checkServerTrusted bodies are empty, disabling certificate validation exactly as the rule describes.
Genuine miss: verify() always yields true but through an if/else with both branches returning true, so a pattern keyed on an unconditional single 'return true;' body will not fire.
True positive: explicit setSecure(false) and setHttpOnly(false) on a session cookie are the literal insecure-flag patterns the rule catches.
True positive: a field literally named 'password' assigned a string literal, plus an AWS-access-key-format literal (AKIA...) and a JDBC connection string embedding a password, all match the rule.
True positive: a Slack token literal (xoxb-...), a Google API key literal (AIza...), and suspiciously-named fields (apiKey/secret) each independently trigger the hardcoded-secret rule.
prepareStatement receives a constant literal and the tainted id reaches the DB only through a setString bind parameter, never the query text.
executeQuery receives a fully constant string literal with no taint source anywhere in the method.
The tainted dir only drives a branch comparison; sql is assigned exclusively constant literals, so executeQuery never receives tainted data.
Integer.parseInt is a listed sanitizer, so the concatenated accountId is untainted before reaching executeQuery.
ESAPI encodeForSQL is a listed encodeForX sanitizer, so the concatenated value is untainted when it reaches executeQuery.
createQuery receives a constant HQL literal and the tainted email is supplied only via a named setParameter bind, never concatenated into the query.
The tainted key is only a map lookup argument (taint through maps is not propagated) and every value returned is a constant literal, so sql is untainted.
executeQuery is a method on a plain Map-backed repository, not java.sql.Statement, and no SQL string ever reaches a query sink, so JSEC-SQLI must not fire on the name alone.
The only executable getInstance call uses SHA-256 (not MD5/SHA-1) and the MD5/exec strings appear solely inside a comment, so JSEC-HASH and JSEC-CMDI have no real sink.

Cipher.getInstance uses authenticated AES/GCM (no DES/3DES/RC4/Blowfish/ECB) and randomness comes from SecureRandom rather than java.util.Random or Math.random, so JSEC-CIPHER and JSEC-RANDOM stay clean.
The factory .newInstance() is immediately hardened with disallow-doctype-decl and external-entity setFeature calls, which is exactly the condition that suppresses JSEC-XXE.
Both cookie flags are set to true (setSecure(true)/setHttpOnly(true)), which is the secure configuration and the inverse of the false-argument pattern JSEC-COOKIE flags.
The File/FileInputStream argument derives from a hardcoded constant path with no request/env/args source, and JSEC-PATH requires taint (not a mere file API), so nothing fires.
ProcessBuilder is constructed from a fixed literal argument list with no attacker-controlled input reaching command(), so JSEC-CMDI has no tainted flow to report.
Engine-review repro: taint flows through a variable-rooted StringBuilder selector chain sb.append(...).append(source).toString().
